newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Should you buy the new real bonds?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Should you buy the new real bonds?.

text.p: In the next two weeks, the U.S. Treasury will bestow its belated New Year's present: the so-called "real" bonds that will be indexed to inflation.

Buy one of these, and the money investors put down is protected against occurrences such as an OPEC oil embargo or the Hunt brothers buying up silver, or prices shaking off their 15 years of moderation and taking off for the sun.

It could happen: inflation was 13.5 percent in 1980 and probably will reinvigorate itself at some point when everyone has stopped worrying about it altogether. Does that make these inflation-proof bonds, priced for the little guy, a good deal?
Not necessarily.
Because of taxes and the low returns they can expect, investors may end up paying a higher price for the guarantee than it is worth.
On January 21 the Treasury plans to announce the amounts to be auctioned in its first index bond offering. The auction will take place on January 29, with trades settling on February 6.

The bonds can be bought through many 401(k) plans, through a broker or from the Treasury Department directly, by contacting a local Federal Reserve Bank or writing to the Bureau of the Public Debt, Washington 20239-0001.

The bonds will be sold in denominations as little as $1,000. They'll pay interest that is generally estimated to be around three percent a year, and they'll also make good on their inflation-matching claims by adding to principal every year to make sure it paces the general rate of price changes.

So, if an investor puts $1,000 into one of these bonds this January, and inflation runs at four percent for the year, the first year's earnings will look like this: $30 interest, payable in two semi-annual instalments, and $40 in inflation-matching interest added to the principal.
POTENTIAL TAX PROBLEMS

The money won't be seen until the bond is cashed. And that's where the tax problems compound. According to John Ziegelbauer, a senior manager in the Washington office of Grant Thornton, a national accounting firm, the interest on principal that the investor doesn't see will be subject to federal income taxes every year when it is posted to his or her account.

That means that, if investors are depending on the bonds for current income, they could have years when the income actually received is less than the taxes due on it and the so-called "phantom" income.
How big a problem is that? Possibly not terrible, says Barbara Moore, a senior vice president at SEI Investments in New York, who has done the calculations.

If the investor is in the lowest 15 percent tax bracket, inflation would have to reach 19 percent before his or her tax bill outstripped their annual earnings payout. If the investors are in the more common 28 percent bracket, that relationship would go against them at an 8.5 percent inflation rate. Those in the 31 percent tax bracket would pay more than they would take in once inflation topped 7.3 percent, and the top 36 percent bracket would suffer at five percent inflation.
Clearly they are a better deal for taxpayers in the lower tax brackets.

But, Moore notes: "If inflation does hit that eight percent level, even if you have to pay out your current taxes, you're going to be very happy you own real bonds." According to Moore, only these inflation-proof bonds will act as real ballast in the event of a stock market meltdown.

Everything else, with the probable exception of real estate, fuels, metals and other commodities, will slump in a period of high inflation. The principal investors hold in traditional bonds will decline when inflation rises as higher interest rates cut the prices on those bonds.
Only "real" bonds will offer real diversification, Moore suggests.
WHAT SORT OF INVESTOR DO THEY APPEAL TO?
So, do investors need or want that diversification?
If they have a long investment horizon and are not the kind of person who looses sleep over investments, these bonds aren't suitable.

But if they are conservative and want to balance the stocks in their portfolio with bonds, this is a better balance than a traditional bond. They might want to put these bonds in a tax-deferred retirement account so they won't have to worry about annual taxes on the principal additions.
Or they may just reason that, since these bonds are already exempt from state and local taxes, it's not worth worrying too much about the federal taxes.
After all, once the bond in cashed, all that extra interest will come back to them. They will have already paid taxes on it, so they won't have to pay them in a big chunk on the bond's sale.
The bottom line? A half-hearted endorsement. These bonds offer protection at a fairly high price. Investors can do better, but can surely do worse.
